text: From finding a service to booking and returning
Redesigned the customer website, from service categories and details to cart and booking, using test feedback and transaction observations to revisit design decisions.
Reviews and testing with the PO and team
Q-CHANG design overview — artwork illustrating the scope of the work
01 / Start with what people want to do
02 / Found the service. Where are the promotions?
03 / One service, with options in one place
04 / Convenience also needs a reason to use it
05 / Less repeated entry for returning customers
Start with what people want to do

I inherited the existing website while both the brand and the back-office system were changing. The first problem was the large number of service categories, which customers struggled to distinguish and find. I began with labels broad enough to cover related services, but specific enough for people to recognize where their needs belonged.
Roof services therefore had different entry points based on intent: repairing a leaking roof or adding a roof extension. People could choose what they wanted to do before choosing a specific service.
The panel above illustrates the categorization principle; it is not a product screenshot.
Found the service. Where are the promotions?

I reviewed the design with the PO and team, then we tested it with approximately 10–12 participants recruited through acquaintances and referrals. We began with unguided exploration, followed by tasks such as finding help for a leaking roof or a dirty air conditioner.

We observed no difficulty using the category tabs for the assigned tasks, but participants asked, “Where are the promotions?” I adjusted both the entry point and the space used to communicate promotions.
Added an all-promotions button at the top
Increased the height of the hero section
Added a clear next-step CTA to the banner
In the follow-up test, the same questions about the location of promotions did not recur. Participants began scrolling through other sections and said the page addressed their home-service needs.
These are qualitative observations from the test group, not conversion results. The individual effects of the changes cannot be separated from this evidence.
One service, with options in one place

Previously, one service was split into separate listings by size and price. I hypothesized that reading many similar listings could be tiring, and grouped the options on one service-detail page — for example, BTU size and price for air-conditioner cleaning.
One service, multiple sizes, multiple listings
One service page, with size and price options together
I used familiar e-commerce patterns, such as choosing shoe size and color on one page, as a reference. The observed trial went well, but there are no before-and-after measurements of time or errors.
Convenience also needs a reason to use it

The shared cart came later because it affected several back-office systems. The hypothesis was that it would help customers buying multiple services; interview participants described it as convenient.

After launch, the transactions the team reviewed showed that customers usually booked just one service. Cross-service purchases, such as air-conditioner cleaning together with house cleaning, were uncommon.
Calling something “convenient” does not tell us how often customers will have a reason to use it.
The team kept the cart and moved on to support returning customers, without concluding that the cart had no value or claiming a measured effect on sales.
Less repeated entry for returning customers
The same phone numbers appeared across multiple transactions, suggesting repeat bookings. I added saved addresses, the most recently used address, and account information.

Service policy still required a phone number at which the customer could be reached. Selecting an address automatically filled its associated phone number, which the customer could edit before confirming.
I owned UX/UI across the customer journey and reviewed and tested the work with the team. This case does not have measured results for repeat-booking rates or booking duration.
The cover is illustrative artwork. Findings and test observations are based on the designer’s account of the work.

Some documents might not be available, and some information might still be incomplete. We also considered technicians applying after a tiring workday, so we divided the workload into sections.
After-work fatigue was a context the team considered, not a directly measured research finding. Reducing drop-off was the goal, but post-launch results are not available.

Registration was split into five sections. Applicants could complete them separately when ready, leave the app, and return. The overview summarized the information and status of each section.

text: Who is affected when a booking date changes?
Analyzed rescheduling records and made the coordination between customers, technicians, CS/IS, and promotions visible enough for the team to make further decisions.
A simplified illustration of the existing coordination process, not a newly launched automated flow.
02 / A date change moves more than a date
04 / The response went beyond the calendar

The March–May 2022 dataset contained 3,999 rescheduling records: 3,545 staff-assisted and 454 self-service. The volume handled by staff prompted an investigation into the coordination behind each request.
These figures count records during the stated period, not unique customers or outcomes achieved after the design work.
A date change moves more than a date

If the original technician was unavailable, a request could pass through CS to check schedules and the IS team to arrange a replacement, before confirming with the customer. If no team was available, further coordination, another date, or a refund was needed.
This brought the discussion back to people’s availability and the time needed to coordinate, before treating fees as the main solution.

One hypothesis was that a reminder just one day before the appointment might prompt a last-minute change. I proposed a five-day reminder to give customers time to review the appointment and the team time to coordinate.
Proposed reminder timing to allow coordination
Previous reminder timing considered in the hypothesis
The customer and technician need an agreed plan
Five days was a coordination proposal, not a proven optimum. The launch status of the revised SMS and the final fee decision have not been confirmed.
The response went beyond the calendar
I recall the team making changes after the presentation across several areas of communication and service preparation.
CS/IS: scripts explaining date changes and their consequences
Technician team: tighter rules for opening and closing calendar availability
Marketing and field consultants: alignment of promotional dates and technician availability
Technician onboarding: explaining what declared availability means
My role was to analyze and present the problem and possible responses. My manager decided how to proceed, and the relevant teams implemented the changes.
I recall fewer rescheduling requests as a behavioral observation after the rules changed, but there are no before-and-after figures and the effect of each change cannot be isolated.
Original presentation, page 3 — the heading rounds the total to approximately 4,000; the exact reference count is 3,999 records.
The value of the work was to make the coordination problem clear enough for the team to act, while distinguishing my proposals from the changes made by the team.

text: Designed UX/UI for a staff-facing workers’ compensation system, understanding invoice workflows, document checks, and cross-system constraints with BAs, SAs, and developers.
A screen organizing medical expenses and comparing billed, payable, and published prices
01 / Problems within and beyond the screen
02 / Design around the work staff need to do
03 / Make system boundaries clear in the UI
04 / Verify the workflow in testing and training
Problems within and beyond the screen

WCF Digital supports compensation processes for work-related injuries and illnesses. The previous system had accumulated many rules and exceptions, with important knowledge also held in staff members’ experience.

For invoices, staff first prepared documents and calculations in Excel outside the system, then entered the results into WCF. The existing screens were dense and did not fully support how the work was actually done.
Design around the work staff need to do
Gathered requirements directly from experienced claims officers, then worked with BAs, SAs, and developers to translate rules, documents, and states into connected screens.
Organize information by hospital and treatment period
Support multiple invoices or receipts within one case
Compare billed, payable, and published prices
Connect supporting documents with the information being reviewed
An example UI using item categories and price columns to make each type of information clear
Make system boundaries clear in the UI
The work covered WCF interactions and states, and cross-system information coordination with BAs and SAs, including document checks connected to ECPS, a system developed by another company.
I owned the WCF-side screens and helped connect the flow. I did not own the system architecture, develop ECPS or its APIs, or set pricing policy.
Verify the workflow in testing and training

According to the case documentation, Hospital Billing passed SIT and UAT. During testing and training, staff could complete the workflow in WCF, from entering information and classifying expenses to checking prices and issuing documents. The system was handed over.
The confirmed results relate to testing, training, and handover. The scheduled go-live and real-world outcomes, such as time, error rates, and adoption, have not been confirmed.
This case connects domain understanding with design and developer handoff, making system constraints understandable rather than leaving staff to work them out alone.

PEC Smart Asset supports asset management and rental operations. This case focuses on Master Asset: defining the information different asset types need, then connecting it to registration and inspection of individual assets.
A car, a drill, a bag of cement, and a renewable document have different identities, quantities, and lifecycles. One identical form cannot communicate the specific information each task needs.
